props.title: Call Northside 777
props.initialSlug: Reporter fights to clear man jailed for cop killing

sections.content: **Call Northside 777** (1948) pioneered the documentary-noir style, with James Stewart delivering a masterful performance as a cynical Chicago reporter investigating a decade-old murder case. Director Henry Hathaway shot extensively on location in Chicago, bringing gritty authenticity that influenced later true-crime films like **All the President's Men** (1976) and **Zodiac** (2007). The film's methodical focus on procedural details and newspaper investigation techniques established a template for investigative journalism movies, while its semi-documentary approach drew directly from producer Louis de Rochemont's "March of Time" newsreel techniques.

sections.content: The post-WWII period saw a surge in these "semi-documentary" crime films, with directors like Hathaway and Anthony Mann combining noir style with documentary realism. **The Naked City** (1948) took it further by filming entirely on New York streets, while **He Walked by Night** (1948) influenced TV's Dragnet with its focus on police procedures. These films reflected both audience demand for "ripped from the headlines" stories and studios' desire to cut costs by shooting on location rather than building expensive sets. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of True Crime Cinema

The documentary-noir style of **Call Northside 777** (1948) laid groundwork for the modern true crime genre. Its influence can be seen in films like **In Cold Blood** (1967), which used similar black-and-white photography and location shooting to create authenticity. The film's focus on journalistic investigation directly influenced later works like **Spotlight** (2015) and **The Post** (2017), showing how dogged reporting can expose injustice and overturn wrongful convictions.
